title: Buttons in a Collector’s Tin
description: Sort a collection of clothing buttons through their shapes, attachment methods, and decorative materials.
cardDescription: Sort a collection of clothing buttons through their shapes, attachment methods, and decorative materials.
focus: A button can be attached through face holes or through a projecting shank. The clues distinguish that fastening structure from the button’s material and the container storing it.
solvingTip: Use the attachment method before the material or shape word.
words: SHANK
Projecting loop on the back of a button for sewing it on
TOGGLE
Long narrow fastening piece passed through a loop
BAKELITE
Early synthetic resin used for some collectible buttons
PEARL
Mother-of-___, iridescent shell material used in buttons
DISC
Flat round shape of many shirt buttons
BUTTON
Small garment fastener collected in this tin
HOLE
Opening through which sewing thread can pass
THREAD
Fine strand attaching a button to cloth
TIN
Metal container holding the small collection
CARD
Backing on which a matched set of buttons may be mounted
LOOP
Curved opening receiving a toggle fastener
SIZE
Measurement distinguishing a coat button from a tiny shirt one
COLOR
Hue used to group the collector's finds
RIM
Outer edge of a circular button

answerNotes.SHANK: A shank provides an attachment below the button face; another design uses holes through the face itself.
answerNotes.TOGGLE: A toggle has a barlike shape rather than the flat disk form of many buttons.
answerNotes.BAKELITE: Bakelite is a material name associated with phenolic resin; not every old plastic button is made from it.
answerNotes.PEARL: Mother-of-pearl is shell material rather than a round loose pearl gemstone.
answerNotes.DISC: Disc describes shape, while the shank or holes describe the attachment arrangement.

title: Glassware in a Display Cabinet
description: Look at collectible glass through its surface effects, supporting foot, and familiar vessel shapes.
cardDescription: Look at collectible glass through its surface effects, supporting foot, and familiar vessel shapes.
focus: Glass collectors distinguish material effects from shapes and manufacturing marks. The clues identify those features without claiming a color or pattern proves an object’s age or value.
solvingTip: Separate a surface appearance from a vessel part or a production mark.
words: OPALESCENT
Having a milky or shifting opal-like appearance, as some glass does
PONTIL
Glassworker's supporting rod whose attachment can leave a base mark
MILKGLASS
Opaque white decorative glass, with spaces omitted
ETCH
To make a surface design by controlled chemical or abrasive removal
FOOT
Supporting base beneath a stemmed glass vessel
BOWL
Rounded upper holding part of a stemmed glass
VASE
Vessel used for displaying cut flowers
RIM
Top edge around a glass vessel's opening
STEM
Narrow support between a glass bowl and foot
TINT
Faint coloring within a piece of glass
CLEAR
Transparent and without strong visible coloration
AMBER
Yellow-brown color found in many glass objects
PINK
Rosy color used in some decorative glassware
MARK
Manufacturer's symbol or other identifying impression
TRAY
Flat support holding small glass pieces in a cabinet

answerNotes.OPALESCENT: Opalescent describes an optical appearance; it does not by itself date or authenticate a glass object.
answerNotes.PONTIL: A pontil mark relates to manufacture; not every mark or rough spot proves the same process or age.
answerNotes.MILKGLASS: Milk glass is an appearance category rather than glass containing dairy milk.
answerNotes.ETCH: Etching changes the surface rather than applying an ordinary painted layer on top.
answerNotes.FOOT: The foot supports the object; the stem joins it to the bowl above.

title: A Music Box on the Shelf
description: Explore a mechanical music box through its pinned cylinder, tuned teeth, and winding mechanism.
cardDescription: Explore a mechanical music box through its pinned cylinder, tuned teeth, and winding mechanism.
subtheme: A Music Box on the Shelf
focus: In a familiar cylinder music box, projecting pins pluck tuned metal teeth. The clues distinguish the part carrying the pattern from the comb producing the notes.
solvingTip: Use the source of motion or sound to identify each component.
words: CYLINDER
Pinned rotating drum carrying a tune pattern in one music-box design
COMB
Row of tuned metal teeth plucked inside a music box
PIN
Small projection on a music-box drum that plucks a tuned tooth
GOVERNOR
Mechanism regulating a music box's running speed
SPRING
Coiled part storing energy when a music box is wound
KEY
Small turning tool used to wind the mechanism
TUNE
Melody played by the mechanical box
DISK
Round patterned plate used by another music-box design
GEAR
Toothed wheel transferring motion inside the mechanism
TOOTH
One tuned metal projection in the musical comb
LID
Hinged upper cover on a music-box case
CASE
Protective outer housing around the mechanism
CRANK
Handle turned to operate some small mechanical music boxes
NOTE
Single musical pitch sounded by a vibrating tooth

answerNotes.CYLINDER: A cylinder carries the arrangement; other music boxes use interchangeable disks instead.
answerNotes.COMB: The comb produces notes when its teeth vibrate; it is not a grooming tool in this scene.
answerNotes.PIN: A pin triggers a note at a position in the tune pattern.
answerNotes.GOVERNOR: A governor helps control the speed, while the spring supplies the stored energy.
answerNotes.SPRING: The spring powers the mechanism as it unwinds rather than generating new energy while running.

title: Shells Arranged in a Cabinet
description: Examine a shell collection through familiar mollusk groups, coiled forms, and labels beside the specimens.
cardDescription: Examine a shell collection through familiar mollusk groups, coiled forms, and labels beside the specimens.
focus: A shell’s shape can help describe its animal group. The clues distinguish a two-valved shell from a coiled gastropod shell and name parts used in a collector’s description.
solvingTip: Start with a familiar shell name, then use the opening or coil terms for crossings.
words: COWRIE
Glossy often oval shell with a long narrow opening
BIVALVE
Mollusk group with two hinged shell halves
GASTROPOD
Mollusk group containing snails and slugs
OPERCULUM
Plate closing the opening of many marine snail shells
WHORL
One complete turn in a coiled shell
SPIRE
Tapered upper portion of a coiled shell
APEX
Pointed tip at the earliest part of a coiled shell
CLAM
Familiar two-shelled mollusk represented in collections
WHELK
Marine snail with a familiar spiral shell
CONCH
Marine snail name associated with a large spiral shell
SCALLOP
Bivalve with a fan-shaped ribbed shell
TRAY
Shallow support holding sorted shell specimens
LABEL
Written identification placed beside a shell
BOX
Small container protecting a collected specimen

answerNotes.COWRIE: A cowrie's smooth surface is natural shell material rather than porcelain.
answerNotes.BIVALVE: Clams and scallops are bivalves; a coiled snail belongs to another mollusk group.
answerNotes.GASTROPOD: Gastropods include both shelled snails and slugs, so a coiled shell is not universal in the group.
answerNotes.OPERCULUM: An operculum is a closing plate, not one of a clam's two valves.
answerNotes.WHORL: A whorl is a turn in the coil; the spire includes several turns toward the tip.

title: A Pocket Watch in Its Case
description: Look inside a traditional pocket watch through its winding controls, timekeeping mechanism, and carrying chain.
cardDescription: Look inside a traditional pocket watch through its winding controls, timekeeping mechanism, and carrying chain.
subtheme: A Pocket Watch in Its Case
focus: A mechanical watch stores energy in a spring and releases it through a regulated mechanism. The clues distinguish the display, its protective case, and the small parts controlling motion.
solvingTip: Separate an outside carrying feature from an internal moving or supporting component.
words: ESCAPEMENT
Watch mechanism controlling the release of energy to the timekeeper
BALANCE
Oscillating wheel helping regulate a mechanical watch
CROWN
Small outside control used to wind or set many watches
JEWEL
Hard bearing insert reducing wear at a watch pivot
FOB
Small attachment or short chain associated with a pocket watch
CASE
Protective outer housing around a pocket watch
LID
Hinged cover protecting some watch dials
DIAL
Marked face on which a watch displays time
HAND
Pointer indicating an hour or minute
CHAIN
Linked attachment securing a pocket watch to clothing
KEY
Separate winding tool used by some older watches
SPRING
Coiled energy store inside a mechanical watch
GEAR
Toothed wheel transferring rotation within a watch
TICK
Repeated small sound associated with the mechanism

answerNotes.ESCAPEMENT: An escapement meters the gear train's motion in coordination with an oscillator rather than simply letting the spring unwind freely.
answerNotes.BALANCE: The balance moves back and forth; it is distinct from a display hand rotating around the dial.
answerNotes.CROWN: A crown is one control design; some older pocket watches instead use a separate key.
answerNotes.JEWEL: Watch jewels are often synthetic ruby and serve a mechanical function rather than merely decoration.
answerNotes.FOB: Fob refers to a carrying attachment in this scene, not a part of the timekeeping mechanism.
